card.profile: Raut Nacha is a traditional dance of the Raut caste, primarily found in the Indian state of Chhattisgarh and neighboring regions. Performed during Diwali, the dance involves men singing and dancing in groups while carrying sticks in village pathways. Historically, the Raut community was involved in cattle herding and milking, and their men also performed the local folk epic Candaini. Today, while the tradition remains anchored in the community, participants from other backgrounds have also begun to take part.
card.insight: Performed during Diwali, Raut Nacha features men dancing in village pathways with sticks while preserving the ancient folk epic Candaini.
card.profile_long:
Raut Nacha is a traditional folk dance rooted in the cultural practices of the Raut caste in India. The Rauts are primarily found in the state of Chhattisgarh, as well as the neighbouring states of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra. Historically, their distribution was concentrated in specific districts including Durg, Raipur, Bastar, Nagpur, and Bhandara. Traditionally, the Rauts were involved in herding and milking cattle, with their main business centered around the sale of milk and milk products. Their historical origins may trace back to a tribal militia in Chhota Nagpur, originating from the Kawar.

As a community tradition, Raut Nacha is performed annually on the festival of Diwali. During this performance, the Rauts wear a special costume and engage in group singing and dancing while holding sticks in their hands, moving through the village pathways. In addition to the dance itself, Raut men traditionally performed the local folk epic Candaini, also known as Chandaini, through a combination of dance and song. This epic narrates the story of princess Chanda, who leaves her impotent husband and falls in love with a common man named Veer Lorik. Both characters belong to the Raut caste, indicating the epic's deep origins within the community. While these performances were historically carried out primarily by Raut men as late as 1980, participants from other communities now also take part.

Over the 20th century, the Raut community underwent Sanskritisation, adopting the customs and values of high-caste Hindus. Sub-castes within the Raut community include Gawala, Thetwar, Jheriya, and Kosariya, and they exist alongside related castes and sub-castes such as the Ahir, Brajwasi, Gawli, Gawali, Lingayat-Gaoli, Gowari, Yadav, Thethwar, and Gop. While detailed technical descriptions of footwork, musical instrumentation, and movement counts are not documented in current sources, the tradition remains a vivid expression of community identity, history, and festive celebration in central India.
